items.value: Only statements 2 and 3 follow: food loss degrades land (hurting land productivity) and reducing it lowers the carbon footprint
items.reasoning: Statement 1 fails on the word 'solely' — the passage says food is lost 'throughout the supply chain, from initial agricultural production to final household consumption', so distribution is one link among many, not the sole cause. Statement 4 asserts that post-harvest technologies are 'not available', which the passage never says. Statement 2 follows from 'the increasing wastage also results in land degradation by about 45%', and statement 3 from 'the energy spent over wasted food results in about 3·5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide production every year'. Since 1 and 4 are both out, only option B survives.

items.value: Only assumption 1 is valid — that the food distribution mechanism needs to be made effective to cut food loss
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 imports a moral claim — that reducing food waste is 'a social and moral responsibility of all citizens' — which appears nowhere in the passage; the passage argues from land degradation, carbon emissions and food sustainability, not from duty. Assumption 1 is the unstated premise behind 'Food is lost or wasted throughout the supply chain' combined with 'Addressing the loss and wastage of food in all forms is critical'; distribution is one of those forms. Runner-up is D (Neither): D wins if one insists the passage never singles out the distribution mechanism as needing reimagining, naming only the supply chain as a whole.

items.value: Both inferences hold — central banks need fiscal backing to disinflate, and monetary policy's effect depends on fiscal policy
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is stated almost directly: 'Without the fiscal backup, monetary policy eventually loses traction.' Statement 1's absolute 'cannot' is licensed by the next sentence, which is categorical: 'Higher interest rates become inflationary, not disinflationary, because they simply lead governments to borrow more to pay rising debt-service costs.' If rate hikes turn inflationary in the absence of fiscal support, the central bank cannot bring inflation down without budgetary backing. Both follow, so C.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid — the passage neither blames fiscal policy alone for higher prices nor says anything about long-term bonds
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 fails on 'solely': the passage treats inflation as the setting in which fiscal and monetary policy interact, and expressly discusses central bank interest-rate action as a cause of outcomes, so fiscal policy is not presented as the sole cause of higher prices. Assumption 2 concerns long-term government bonds, a subject the passage never touches — it mentions borrowing and debt-service costs but says nothing about bond maturities or their behaviour under higher prices. Neither is assumed, so D.

items.value: 9 cuts
items.reasoning: 64 identical pieces from a cube means a 4 × 4 × 4 array of small cubes. Producing 4 equal divisions along one axis requires 3 parallel planar cuts, and this must be done along each of the three mutually perpendicular axes: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. Fewer cuts cannot produce 64 pieces that are all identical cubes, and 9 is the smallest option that is achievable.

items.value: 0, achieved by 5 − 4 − 3 + 2 × 1
items.reasoning: Exhaustive enumeration of all 4-operator fillings from {+, −, ×} that use no symbol more than twice, evaluated with normal precedence, gives 0 as the least non-negative value: 5 − 4 − 3 + 2 × 1 = 5 − 4 − 3 + 2 = 0, using '−' twice, '+' once and '×' once, all within the limit. Since 0 is attainable and no value below it is non-negative, the answer is 0.

Men and days are inversely proportional for a fixed amount of work, so men × days is constant: M × 6k = M' × 5k, giving M' = (6/5)M irrespective of the value of k. The increase is (6/5)M − M = M/5, i.e. 20% of the original number of men.

items.value: 6 hours 45 minutes
items.reasoning: Take the job as 24 units: X does 4 units/hour, Y and Z do 3 each. Since no one may work two consecutive hours, X — the fastest — can work at most in alternate hours, so in any 6 hours the most that can be done is 3 X-hours plus 3 other-hours = 3(4) + 3(3) = 21 units. Work done by time 6 + f is therefore at most 21 + 4f, and 21 + 4f = 24 gives f = 3/4. A schedule such as X, Y, X, Z, X, Y then X for 45 minutes attains this bound exactly, so the minimum is 6 hours 45 minutes.

items.value: 200 zeros
items.reasoning: The product is the n-th term n^(2n) for n = 1 to 25. The power of 5 comes only from n = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, contributing 2n times the power of 5 in n: 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 100 = 200. The power of 2 summed the same way over the even n comes to 608. The number of terminal zeros is min(608, 200) = 200.

items.value: 8th January, 2023, when the total is ₹64 = 8² = 4³
items.reasoning: Daily savings are 1, 3, 5, 7, … so the total after n days is the sum of the first n odd numbers, namely n². For n² to be a perfect cube as well, n must itself be a perfect cube. Within the choices, n = 8 gives 64, which is both 8² and 4³. The 7th (49) and the 9th (81) are squares but not cubes, so B. (The stem prints 'a perfect square as well a perfect cube', with 'as' missing; the sense is unaffected.)

items.value: Urban planning curricula should be diverse and interdisciplinary
items.reasoning: The passage attributes the success of New York, London and Paris to the systems approach, then explains that Western planners were expert in computing, statistics, optimization and algorithmic problem-solving because 'these very subjects were absorbed into the planning curriculum that had its roots in the social sciences, geography and architecture' — an explicitly interdisciplinary mix — and closes by noting that Indian planning education differs. Option A is the only inference drawn from what is on the page; B, C and D each introduce facts about Indian bureaucracy, municipal finance and urban poverty that the passage never mentions.

items.value: Only assumption 1 is valid — India needs urban professionals equipped for modern urban practice
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 fails on its absolute: 'no capacity or potential' to impart systems-approach training is a far stronger claim than 'Planning in India, and its education differ from the West', which reports a difference, not an incapacity. Assumption 1 is the unstated premise that makes the closing contrast meaningful — the West's iconic cities came from professionals trained this way, and India's education differs, so India needs such professionals. Runner-up is D (Neither): D wins if one holds that noting a difference presupposes no deficiency at all, so that even assumption 1 goes beyond the text.

items.value: Social media are commercial products built for profit, not ideal or moral institutions
items.reasoning: The passage's two working claims are that capital buys a louder voice ('anonymous private entities with high capital can pay for more space for their opinions') and that platforms promote whatever maximises engagement 'regardless of how inflammatory the content may be'. Both describe commercial logic overriding public good, which is exactly option B. A and D praise social media in terms the passage does not use, and C is contradicted by the observation that political discourse and 'the quality of politics suffers'.

items.value: Both are valid — the internet is not inclusive enough, and it can damage the quality of politics
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 is nearly explicit: 'If political discourse in the digital sphere is a matter of outshining one's opponent till the election is won, then the quality of politics suffers.' Assumption 1 rests on the opening pair of sentences — 'Not every voice on the internet commands the same kind of audience' and those with capital 'are effectively buying a louder voice' — which is a statement of unequal participation, i.e. insufficient inclusiveness. Runner-up is B (2 only): B wins if 'inclusive' is read narrowly as access to the platform rather than equality of reach, since the passage concerns amplification and not who may speak at all.

items.value: Divisible by 3 and 37 but not by 2
items.reasoning: 222 = 2 × 3 × 37 and 333 = 3² × 37, so both bases are multiples of 3 and of 37; hence both powers, and therefore their sum, are divisible by 3 and by 37. For 2: 222^333 is even but 333^222 is odd (333 is odd), so their sum is odd and not divisible by 2. Direct modular computation confirms the sum is 1 mod 2, 0 mod 3 and 0 mod 37.

items.value: 20% water (20 litres of water per 100 litres of honey)
items.reasoning: Take 100 litres of honey costing ₹100, i.e. ₹1 per litre, and add w litres of water, which costs nothing. The mixture is sold at the cost price of honey, ₹1 per litre, so the revenue is (100 + w) and the profit is w on an outlay of 100, giving a profit of w%. Setting w% = 20% gives w = 20, so 20% water must be mixed with the honey.

30^30 = 3^30 × 10^30, so the number is 3^30 followed by exactly thirty zeros, and the digit immediately preceding those zeros is the last digit of 3^30. The last digit of powers of 3 cycles 3, 9, 7, 1 with period 4, and 30 leaves remainder 2, so the last digit is 9. Direct expansion confirms 30^30 ends in …94649 followed by thirty zeros.

items.value: 3 divisors — namely 2, 3 and 6
items.reasoning: If a divisor d leaves remainder 1 in both cases, then d divides 421 − 1 = 420 and 427 − 1 = 426, so d divides gcd(420, 426) = 6. The divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6, but d = 1 is impossible because a remainder of 1 requires d > 1. That leaves 2, 3 and 6, each of which does leave remainder 1 with both 421 and 427 — three divisors.

items.value: 4 possible bottle sizes — 1, 7, 19 and 133 litres
items.reasoning: A single bottle size must divide 399 exactly and also divide 532 exactly, so it must divide gcd(399, 532). Since 399 = 3 × 7 × 19 and 532 = 2² × 7 × 19, the gcd is 133 = 7 × 19, whose divisors are 1, 7, 19 and 133 — four sizes. Unlike the divisor question about remainders, nothing here excludes 1, because the stem imposes only that the capacity be an integer number of litres.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — the unit digit can be 0 or 5, but never 9
items.reasoning: The primes below 10 are 2, 3, 5 and 7, and choosing three distinct ones gives only four sums: 2+3+5 = 10, 2+3+7 = 12, 2+5+7 = 14 and 3+5+7 = 15. The possible unit digits are therefore 0, 2, 4 and 5. Statement 1 (0) and statement 3 (5) are attainable; statement 2 (9) is not, which eliminates every option except C.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 ranks parents above governments in school education, a comparison the passage never makes — parents appear only as holders of expectations about their children's future. Assumption 2 fails chiefly on 'uniform for the entire country', an idea absent from the text; moreover the passage's complaint is that attainment falls short of the curriculum that already exists ('far lower than they should be even based on curricular expectations of class 8'), so a redesigned curriculum is not what it presupposes. Runner-up is B (2 only): B wins if the uniformity clause is treated as incidental colour and the hedge 'may address' as enough to make a new, contemporary curriculum an implicit remedy.

items.value: Public policy should align young people's competencies and achievements with their expectations
items.reasoning: The passage sets up a single gap: children and parents expect school 'graduates' to move on to high school and college and nobody wants to return to agriculture, yet 'abilities in terms of academic competencies are far lower than they should be'. That mismatch between expectation and attainment is precisely what option C names. A (poverty eradication), B (monetary incentives) and D (returning to agriculture as a condition for the demographic dividend) introduce remedies and claims the passage never advances.

items.value: Science must pursue truth yet also be answerable for social welfare
items.reasoning: The author holds both halves at once: Newton and Galileo acknowledged only the responsibility 'to tell the truth', and the modern addition, which the author endorses as something 'we take for granted', is that 'science has a social responsibility'. Option D is the only choice that keeps truth-seeking and social responsibility together. A misdescribes the point as valuing scientists' commitment, B substitutes 'scientific awareness' for social responsibility, and C reverses the passage's own causal remark that the social sense 'begins at the industrial revolution'.

items.value: A, A, C, D — completing the sequence as AABCD / ABBCD / ABCCD / ABCDD
items.reasoning: The string has twenty places with blanks at positions 2, 6, 14 and 19, and the fixed letters already read A_BCD | _BBCD | ABC_D | ABC_D in blocks of five. Filling with A, A, C, D gives AABCD, ABBCD, ABCCD, ABCDD — each block is ABCD with exactly one letter doubled, and the doubled letter advances A, B, C, D across the four blocks. No other option produces a consistent progression: B yields ABBCD, ABBCD, ABCCD, ABCDD (the doubling repeats at B), and A and D put the doublings out of order.

Since the two shares total ₹2,000 and differ by ₹400, P gets ₹1,200 and Q gets ₹800, a ratio of 3 : 2. Profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time, so with Q's capital q and P's capital q + 14,000 we need 8(q + 14,000) : 10q = 3 : 2, giving 16q + 224,000 = 30q and q = 16,000. P's capital is therefore 16,000 + 14,000 = ₹30,000; checking, 30,000 × 8 = 240,000 against 16,000 × 10 = 160,000, which is 3 : 2.
